title: The Xi'an stele (781)
hookLine: a stone in China records the luminous religion brought by Syriac-speaking monks

lines: A STONE ON A TORTOISE'S BACK.
A CROSS RISING FROM A LOTUS.
CHINESE AND SYRIAC, SIDE BY SIDE.
cards: A tall slab of dark stone stands in a museum in Xi'an, in China, on the back of a carved stone tortoise. At the top, carved small, a cross rises out of clouds and a lotus flower.
Below, columns of Chinese characters run down the face, and along the bottom and edges runs a second script, Syriac, the language of the churches of the East.
The Chinese title calls it a memorial to the spread of the luminous religion in China. It tells how a teaching came east, carried by monks with books.

teach.b: Here's the story the stone tells, in paraphrase. A monk named Alopen came from the West, from a land the Chinese called Daqin, carrying scriptures and images.
He arrived at the capital, Chang'an, the city we now call Xi'an.

teach.h: THE EMPEROR HAS THE BOOKS TRANSLATED.
teach.b: The emperor Taizong sent an official to welcome him, had his scriptures translated in the palace library, questioned him about the teaching, and issued a decree allowing it to be taught. Monasteries were built.
Then the stone sums up the faith, and this part rewards slow reading. One true God. The Messiah born of a virgin.

teach.h: THE WISE MEN, TOLD IN CHINESE.
teach.b: A bright star announcing the birth, and Persians who saw it and came with gifts: the wise men, told in Chinese. Baptism by water, and the cross.

teach.h: BORROWED WORDS FOR A NEW TEACHING.
teach.b: All of it in words borrowed from the religious language already living in China, some Buddhist, some Daoist. The monks didn't invent a new vocabulary. They reached for the words people already prayed with.
Even the name they chose, the luminous teaching, is a word about light. The stone also records hard times, when the community was mocked and opposed, and then renewed favor.
It was carved later than Alopen's arrival, a look back on what had grown. The monks belonged to the Church of the East, and this stone lets that church speak for itself, in two scripts.

This week has gone a long way: Caedmon singing after a dream in the stable, Cuthbert by the sea, Bede finishing his work, then Ethiopia, Armenia, Kerala, and now China. The church of these centuries was not one place.

how: Christians of the Assyrian Church of the East and related churches remember the monks who carried their faith along the Silk Road, and the Xi'an stele is studied and visited as a record of that history.

games.q: you're a monk arriving in a great foreign capital with scriptures nobody there can read. how do you explain your faith?
o: only in Syriac, and wait for people to learn it.
in the local language, borrowing words people already pray with.
don't explain it. just build a church.
games.why: the stone's Chinese text borrows Buddhist and Daoist words to tell of the Messiah, the star and baptism.

practice: Picture the Silk Road: the Mediterranean on the left, China on the right, deserts, mountains and oasis towns between.
Follow it slowly from west to east, the way a monk with books and a walking stick might have gone, and notice how long it is.
If you pray, pray for the Christians who live along that road today, and for everyone else who lives there too.

wordCard.voice: Alopen. The monk who carried Christian scriptures from the West to the Chinese capital, where the emperor allowed his teaching and monasteries were built.

orig.note: Chinese: the luminous teaching, the name the stone gives the faith.
